items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: When the House resumes on
Tuesday, 22 October, the Government in tends to progress the Telecommunications
(Interception Capability and Security) Bill, the Members of Parliament (Remuneration
and Services) Bill, and the Health and Safe ty (Pike River Implementation) Bill. With
the agreement of the Business Committee, th e sitting on Tuesday, 22 October will be
extended on the morning of 23 October, and the House will consider the Te Urewera-
Tūhoe Bill, the Ng āti Hauā Claims Settlement Bill, the Ng āti Koroki Kahukura Claims
Settlement Bill, and the Mokomoko (Restora tion of Character, Mana, and Reputation)
Bill. Wednesday, 23 October is a members’ day.
Hon John Banks—Ministerial Resignation
1. GRANT ROBERTSON (Labour—Wellington Central) to the Prime Minister:
Does he stand by his statement yesterday that Hon John Banks is a “credible” and
“trustworthy” individual?
Hon BILL ENGLISH (Deputy Prime Minister)  on behalf of the Prime Minister:
Yes.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: If he believes that John Banks  is a credible and trustworthy
individual, why did he accept his resignation as a Minist er, given that Mr Banks
continues to insist he has done nothing wrong and has nothing to fear, nothing to hide?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Because Mr Banks indicated to the office of the Prime
Minister late last week that in the event the judge ruled against him he would tender his
resignation as a Minister. The judge ruled ag ainst him, he kept his word, and tendered
his resignation as a Minister.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Given his statement yesterday th at he would reinstate Mr Banks
as a Minister if he managed to avoid a tria l, can he confirm that he regards Mr Banks’
conduct as acceptable for Ministers who are part of his Government?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The member has misrepresented what the Prime Minister
said yesterday.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Can he confirm that Mr Banks’ actions make him acceptable to
be a Minister in his Government?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, the member may have not iced that Mr Banks is not a
Minister in the current Government.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Is it not the case that the Prime Mi nister is the last person left in
New Zealand who thinks that John Banks is cr edible and trustworthy, and that he is
saying that only because he desperately needs to  cling to that political corpse to prop up
his Government?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: For the benefit of the member, if he looks at the confidence
and supply agreements, which are publicly av ailable, the Prime Minister commands a
majority of 64 votes to 57 in this Parliame nt. No single vote is critical to the
Government. Secondly, if legal proceedings continue, as indicated  yesterday, and Mr
Banks does go to trial, he will benefit, as every other New Zealand citizen does, from
13998 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2013
the presumption of innocence until prove n guilty. The Labour Party may know the
result already. Fortunately, the legal system is more even handed.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Does he now regret refusing to read the police report into John
Banks filing a false electoral return, given that  he had all the information he needed to
know that Mr Banks should resi gn as a Minister last Sept ember but he failed to act on
it?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. The correct way of hand ling allegations that someone
has not complied with the law is through the legal process.
Hon John Banks—Potential Conflicts of Interest
2. METIRIA TUREI (Co-Leader—Green)  to the Minister for Economic

items.speaker: Development
items.text: Has Cabinet discussed delaying the passage of the New Zealand
International Convention Centre Bill until the Hon John Banks prosecution is resolved;
if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: No. I am relatively
new here, but it is my understanding that th e executive proposes le gislation and then a
properly constituted Parliament of the House of Representatives debates and votes on
legislation. I dare say that is what will actually happen in this case.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Has Cabinet discussed the conflict of interest arising from Mr Banks
having a crucial vote on the Skyc ity deal at the same time as  Skycity is a witness in the
court proceedings against Mr Banks re garding a $15,000 donation that Mr Banks
received from Skycity?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I am not really sure what the member is trying to imply
here, but my understanding is that Parliament gets to vote on legislation. Every member
of Parliament in this House has the opportuni ty to do that, and to vote according to how
their party and their caucus want them to vote. I think that is what is appropriate. It is
generally what occurs, and I am sure that is what will occur in this case.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Sp eaker. My question expressly asked
“Has Cabinet discussed the conflict of interest”—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I agree with the point the member  is raising. Would she please ask
the question again.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Has Cabinet discussed the conflict of interest arising from Mr Banks
having a crucial vote on the Skyc ity deal at the same time as  Skycity is a witness in the
court proceedings against Mr Banks re garding a $15,000 donation that Mr Banks
received from Skycity?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, I reject much of the supposition contained in that
question, but the answer is still no—the same as it was for the primary question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Why does the Minister not believe that  there is a conflict of interest,
when Mr Banks’ seat in this House is po tentially dependent on the evidence that
Skycity will present at his criminal trial, and Skycity’s $400 million deal could stand or
fall on Mr Banks’ vote?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Well, this Parliament is the master of its own destiny, and
every MP who sits here sits he re because of this Parliament  and are entitled to do so.
While they are here, I presume they are entitle d to vote. I might be old-fashioned in that
respect, but that was my understanding of it.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! This is a point of order, and it will be—[Interruption] Order!
A point of order has been called, and there were interjections coming from two quarters
of the House. If that con tinues, you leave me with no choice but to ask the member
interjecting through a point of order to leave the Chamber.
17 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 13999

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Again, my question expressly con cerned whether he believed there
was or was not a—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I listened care fully to the question, a nd on this occasion the
Minister addressed it to my satisfaction.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister be lieve it is good for democracy to pass a law
benefiting Skycity while relying on the vote of a man whose seat in this House, and
even his freedom, may depend on the testimony that Skycity presents at his criminal
trial?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Speaking to the question, there are two answers to it.
Firstly, I disagree with the member’s characte risation of the benefits  of the legislation.
The benefit of this legislation is to the people of Auckland and to the people of New
Zealand, who would obtain a $400 million convention centre for the benefit of
economic growth and jobs in this country. I know that member disagrees, but it is
democratic for people to have different views.

items.speaker: Hon Dr Nick Smith
items.text: What reports has the Minister received on the precedent that
was set when retrospective legislation for paying for credit card costs in the 2005
election came before Parliament, in whic h every member of the Government had a
vested interest—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I cannot see how that could possi bly be relevant to the primary
question.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I agree with the member.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does the Minister think that a Government deal that causes people
harm in order to increase casino profits is morally bankrupt?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I completely disagree with the premise of that member’s
question, and here is the problem. The tenor of the questions of the member today is
that she does not want a properly constituted Pa rliament of this country to vote on this
legislation because she disagrees with it. I am sorry, but that is wrong.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Will the Minister meet with the victims of problem gambling and
explain to them why he feels comfortable using the vote of a disgraced MP to pass a law
that will increase the harm that problem gambling causes to our communities?

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: Everybody has a different view on what is disgraceful, and
I think it is actually reasonabl y disgraceful to run a politic al campaign with taxpayers’
money during a term, but that is just my view. Of course, what  is allowed to be done is
allowed to be done. But my view on that is that every human activity involves some risk
and every risk has to be managed, and that is what happens. The member, unless she is
proposing to ban casinos and ban all gambling and ban lotteries, has no right to lecture
me on that subject.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. I expressly asked the Minister
whether he will meet with the victims of—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The question was far more loaded than that.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is this not the truth of the matte r, Minister, that the Skycity bill—
[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! The member has a right to ask a supplementary question.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Is it not the truth of the matter that the Skycity bill is a sleazy deal in
which his Government trades harm—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! That question is now out of order.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I just want to check, first of all, that the member is not going to
question the decision I have just made.
14000 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2013

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: No, I am not going to questio n your decision. I would like your
reasoning as to why you now consider that question out of order. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I do not need assistance. The member can just go back and
look at the wording of her question and some of the words she used in that question, and
I am sure she will figure it out for herself.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just again clarify that we  are not in any way questioning a
ruling.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I am not questioning your decision.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Then I will hear a fresh point of order.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Does your ruling now mean that the word “sleazy” is a prohibited
word in this Parliament?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, it does not.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Can I just remind the member, because she is getting very, very
close to having to be asked to leave the Chamber, that if she continues to raise points of
order that I consider are trifling with th e Chair, Speakers’ rulings—Speaker’s ruling
20/8, from memory—will suggest that she leaves me with no choice.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I understand.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: OK, we will hear one more—hopefully one more—point of order.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: At the point that you declared my question out of order, which is
your right to do so, the only phrase I had used was “sleazy deal”. I am not sure—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! The member will resume her seat. I
have ruled the question out of order. That is the end of th e matter. It is not something
that is relitigated in this House.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. It has been the practice under
your term as Speaker for members, both of the Government and of Opposition parties,
to seek clarification from you on rulings. It is  a perfectly legitimate part of all the time
that I have been in the Cham ber that that has been done, a nd that when a ruling appears
to be a new one, members have the right to  raise points of order with you and you have
in the past responded. Or, if not that day, you come back with a considered ruling to
explain why you made the ruling you made. I think that would be the appropriate course
in this case.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: And I agree with the member. Meti ria Turei raised the question as
to whether “sleazy” was now an unparliamentary term, and I said no.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I will hear, but I just want to warn the member that if we are any
way addressing a decision I have made, I will be immediately, sadly, asking the member
to leave the Chamber.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: Absolutely, Mr Speaker. My point of order to you—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I just want to check that it is a fresh point of order.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: It is a fresh point of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Good.

items.speaker: Metiria Turei
items.text: What part of my question was out of order?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The member will now leave the Chamber. [ Interruption] Order! I
am on my feet.
Metiria Turei withdrew from the Chamber.

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I ask—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! We have a point of order, and it will be heard in silence.
[Interruption] Order!
17 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14001

items.speaker: Iain Lees-Galloway
items.text: I ask that you reflect on the original decision to rule Metiria
Turei’s question out of order and perhaps br ing a considered response back to the
House. You have now left members in a difficult situation, I submit, in that it is difficult
to craft questions that are in order because we do not know why it was that Metiria
Turei’s question was out of order.

items.speaker: Hon Anne Tolley
items.text: I suggest that every member in this House has a responsibility to
read the Standing Orders. If you read Standing Order 377, it makes it very clear.
Standing Order 377(1)(b) states: “arguments, in ferences, imputations, epithets, ironical
expressions or expressions of opinion,”—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I thank the member. I do not need further help on this point.
Iain Lees-Galloway—[Interruption] Order! Iain Lees-Galloway has asked a reasonable
question. I will have a further consideration of  it, but I again say ex actly what I said to
Metiria Turei. I think that a reread of th e supplementary question that was asked would
help the member understand. But I do want to point out that Metiria Turei was not asked
to leave the House because she asked that  question. She continue d to raise numerous
points of order that were relitigating—[ Interruption] Order! I am on my feet. She
continued to raise numerous points of order th at were, in effect, re litigating a decision
the Speaker had made.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I seek clarification,
and it is simply this. It is  not to challenge your ruli ng, but to ask you whether the
statement that rules out that word is a precedent, or is it based on a precedent?

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: No, again, the member is now ra ising exactly the same point of
order that was raised by Metiria Turei—whether the word “sleazy” is unparliamentary. I
said that, no, it was not necessarily unparliamentary. It was the total content of the
question that I was not satisfied with.
Infrastructure Investment Programme—Progress and Future Investment Fund

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: What progress is the
Government making with its multi-billion dollar—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry, that question wa s very difficult to hear at the
start because of the level of interjection. Would the member start again?
3. NICKY WAGNER (National—Christchurch Central)  to the Minister of

items.speaker: Finance
items.text: What progress is the Government making with its multi-billion dollar
infrastructure investment programme, as part of its wider plan to build a more
productive and competitive economy?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The 2013 National State of
Infrastructure report issued today shows that the Government is making good progress.
It shows a pipeline of around $14 billion worth of investment, including large
investments in electricity transmission; the roll-out of ultra-fast broadband; and major
transport projects, including roads of nati onal significance, completion of the Auckland
metropolitan rail network, begun under the pr evious Government, and the KiwiRail
Turnaround Plan. It also shows that regulatory changes made by this Government to the
relevant statutes have enabled 13 large projects to be cons ented in recent years, when
this would normally have taken up to 7 years.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: Why has the Government made investment in modern infrastructure
a high priority within its wider economic programme?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It has made an investment because we have a very optimistic
view about the future for growth in New Zealand, and we want the infrastructure
investment to permit that growth, rather than to smother it. So despite the recession and
a tight financial situation, the Government has set out on a larg e-scale programme,
which, through difficult times in the job mark et, has supported thousands of jobs across
14002 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2013
New Zealand. We have also we lcomed more private sector  involvement in delivering
public infrastructure, and this has been important in improving the efficiency and
effectiveness of this investment.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: What are some of the main areas to benefit from the Government’s
significant investment in infrastructure?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. Standing Order 377(1)(b)
actually applies to all of the questions that Nicky Wagner has asked, and I was
wondering whether you were goin g to rule on either of the first two—that is, questions
must not contain “arguments, inferences, impu tations, epithets, ironical expressions or
expressions of opinion,”. All of  her questions have done th at and they should all be
ruled out of order.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I certainly did not interpret that question in that way. If members
want to get down to adhering strictly to Standing Order 377, I can do that. But it will
hardly make it an interesting—[ Interruption] Order! I ask the member to ask her
question again.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: What are some of the main areas to benefit from the Government’s
significant investment in infrastructure?

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: If the member is going to say that that question is out of order, then
he is wrong.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I am seeking clarification from you about whether speaking about
the benefits of significant investment amounts to a breach of Standing Order 377(1)(b).

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I would have preferre d the question to be asked without the word
“significant”, but I am not ruling the questi on out of order because it included the word
“significant”.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The answer is really a matter of fact rather than opinion. The
significant investments—[Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I am sorry to interrupt the member. That interjection from
Grant Robertson directly questions the impartiality of the Speaker.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Well, that is a very serious inte rjection. The Hon Bill English is to
answer the question.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The investments are significant because they are so large.
There has been a $5.9 billion investment  in roading, $3 billion for rebuilding
Christchurch, $1.7 billion in the health se ctor, $900 million for education, $690 million
for the housing sector, and $430 million for ultra-fast broadband, and these are for just
the years 2012-13 and 2013-14.

items.speaker: Te Ururoa Flavell
items.text: Kia ora t ātou. What can the resident s of Raetihi, Turakina,
Whangaehu, and Whanganui expect to rece ive out of the Government’s multibillion-
dollar infrastructure investme nt programme to support them in facing recent crisis
events such as flooding and diesel spills in their river?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Certainly, in the case of the flooding, there are arrangements
in place between the Government and local councils for a degree of cost-sharing where
that is appropriate. These are provisions that have been in place for up to 10 years and
were used, for instance, in the case of extensive flooding in the Manawat ū a number of
years back. I cannot comment in detail on the di esel spill issue; it would be better to ask
the relevant Minister.

items.speaker: Nicky Wagner
items.text: How will proceeds from the Gove rnment’s share offer programme
to be invested out of the Future Inve stment Fund help to pay for new public
infrastructure?
17 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14003

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: One of the benefits of the Government’s share offers is that
they generate significant amounts of cas h from New Zealanders, who have the
opportunity to invest in large New Zealand companies, and th at cash is paid into the
Government bank account. In the case of Mi ghty River Power it is around $1.7 billion.
We can then use that cash to invest in public infrastructure w ithout having to go and
borrow it from foreign lenders, as any number of  other people would prefer that we do.
In the past two Budgets we have allocated around $2 billion from the Future Investment
Fund into 21st century schools, new hospitals, and the rebuild of Christchurch.
Superannuation Fund—Commentary and Contributions
4. Hon DAVID PARKER (Deputy Leader—Labour)  to the Minister of Finance:
Does he agree with the Dominion Post report that “Bill English was gushing about the
NZ Super Fund yesterday” saying it was “one  of the best-structu red sovereign wealth
funds in the world”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No, I do not agree that I was gushing;
I was simply pointing out wh at is a widely acknowledged fact. As the member may
want to point out to the House, I went on to praise the architect of the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund, Dr Michael Cullen, w ho was the finance spokesman when
Labour had finance spokespeople who knew how to handle Labour’s spending instincts.
That is why he set it up—to protect New Zealand from the Labour caucus—and he did a
great job.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Is it correct that he voted against the New Zealand
Superannuation Fund, voted against the formation of KiwiSaver, as Minister of Finance
halted contributions to the New Zeal and Superannuation Fund, opposes universal
KiwiSaver, and will not address the age of eligibility of New Zealand superannuation?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I am just trying to remember the order, but it goes something
like yes, yes, no, no, yes—I think—to answer any one of those questions. Of course, the
Government has made pragmatic decisions about contributions to the Superannuation
Fund. The fund was designed to make contribu tions when we had surpluses. Dr Cullen
made sure that happened, so that Labour di d not waste them. Unfortunately, we have
had to deal with the legacy of deficits that Labour left behind. When we have cleared up
that mess, we will start making contributions again.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Given that the Guardians of New Zealand Superannuation
estimate that the fund would be a net—that  is, net of the extr a contributions—$2.2
billion better off had he not suspended cont ributions in 2009, is he now prepared to
admit that his suspension of contributions has decreased the wealth of the fund?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: No. In fact, our policy simply  follows the Labour policy as
articulated by David Shearer when he said : “We have listened. That’s why I won’t
continue with [the] previous policy to rest ore contributions to the … Super Fund until
… we can afford it.” That is our policy too.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What were Treasury’s fiscal a nd economic forecasts in late 2008
and into 2009, which influenced the incoming Government’s decision to temporarily
suspend contributions to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The forecasts actually showed that if the Government had
maintained the spending and policy track it had inherited, we would never return to
surplus, and that net Government debt w ould have exceeded 60 percent of GDP by the
early 2020s. Under this Government’s sensible policy, debt will be around 20 percent of
GDP—around one-third of that projected as a result of the Labour Party policies.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: Did the temporary suspension of  contributions to which Mrs
Upston referred begin in 2008, and is it pr edicted to end, under his Government’s
policy, only in 2020?
14004 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2013

items.speaker: Hon Steven Joyce
items.text: Well, if it was Labour it would be 2030.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: My colleague makes a good point. If we followed the
Labour Party policies that we inherited, we would be restor ing contributions in about
2070, because it would have taken that long to ge t debt back to some kind of reasonable
level. I do not think that the member’s pa rty’s policy has changed. His previous leader
said a Labour Government would make cont ributions when the country can afford it.
We think that is reasonable, and we agree with that policy.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. The Minister has no
responsibility for, and should not misrepresent, Labour Party policy.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: The question was around when the—[ Interruption] Order! The
question was really around, firs t of all, when did the contributions conclude, and then,
when they might start again. He is allowed to justify that, in my opinion.

items.speaker: Hon David Parker
items.text: How can he be gushing about the Superannuation Fund when he
voted against it and said at the time that the scheme was “a dog”?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The fact is that at the time there was extensive discussion
over whether the New Zealand Government c ould maintain the surpluses required to
continue making contributions. It turned out that within 4 or 5 years that was not the
case, so I think we were probably half right. On the other half, the fund has turned out to
be well structured, making good returns, and we support its continuation.

items.speaker: Louise Upston
items.text: What reports has he seen setting out sensible approaches to making
contributions to the New Zealand Superannuation Fund?

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: I saw one report that I thought was pretty sensible. It said
that “The government will make contributions to the Fund from available surpluses.
Where these are insufficient for making the required contribution a reduced contribution
would be made.” I would venture to suggest  that if the speaker had contemplated
deficits, he would have said that if th ere were deficits, we probably would not
contribute. That comment came from Dr Mi chael Cullen. I think the legislation was

policy.
Welfare Reforms—Impact
5. MELISSA LEE (National)  to the Minister for Social Development : What
reports has she received on the progress of the Government’s welfare reforms to date?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We are seeing more
people coming off benefits as a result of the Government’s efforts to support more
people off welfare and into work. Benefit nu mbers are at the lowest they have been
since 2008. In the September quarter the numbe r of New Zealanders on benefits fell by
5,388 people to just over 304,000, which is the th ird straight quarterly drop. A year ago
there were almost 321,000 New Zealanders on  benefits. This ha s fallen by 16,500
people since September 2012.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: How is the Government’s new work bonus payment supporting people
to transition into work?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The new work bonus payment allows people who are not
work tested and who go off that benefit an d into work to keep their benefit, which
reduces by $100 a week. In just the 6 w eeks since the new work bonus policy was
introduced, 706 people have come off benefit into work, seeking out and landing jobs,
even though they have no requ irement to work. As I said, th is means that they can keep
their benefit for longer, and it is easier for them to transition to a wage.

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: How are the changes making a difference for people in the regions?
17 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14005

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: We have seen significant drops over the last year, in
particular for sole parents in the Bay of Plenty, where that number is down by 524. In
Canterbury it is down by 721, in the central region it is down by 500, in Waikato it is
down by 689, and in Auckland it is down by ne arly 3,000 people. As for job seekers in
Auckland, there are 4,500 fewer people; in Canterbury the number  is down by 2,162;
and in Mrs Anne Tolley’s own East Coast it is down by 815 people, which is really
significant.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Given her assertion that 2,000 people every week have their benefits
cancelled even though they have  no job to go to, can she guarantee that those 2,000
people and their children are not falling further into poverty?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The number of people who leave for reasons other than
finding work has not changed. It was the same in 2007 as it is now.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I didn’t ask that.

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Well, it is significant. What we have got is people leaving
for the reasons of getting into a relationship, changing benefit categories, or going into
study, so they change benefits. Those numbers have not actually changed in the last 13
years. They leave for many different reasons. Some will do so, as I said, for relationship
reasons and other reasons. What has changed is the number of people who are leaving to
go into work, and, as I have expressed, that has gone up.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr  Speaker. My question was very
straightforward. I asked for a guarantee—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! [ Interruption] Order! I apologise to the member. I was
concentrating on another matte r. I did not hear the quest ion to know whether it was
addressed. I invite the member to ask the question again.

items.speaker: Sue Moroney
items.text: Thank you. Given her assertion that 2,000 people every week have
their benefits cancelled even though they ha ve no job to go to, can she guarantee that
those 2,000 people and their children are not falling further into poverty?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: The assertion of the question is that we cancel 2,000
benefits each week. Those people cancel th em themselves, right? They say they no
longer require a benefit, because they are in  a relationship, because they have gone into
study, or because they have transferred on to another benefit. This may help the
member: since welfare reforms, 37 percent are cancelling into work compared with just
30 percent in 2007.

Welfare Reforms—Evaluation and Individual Case Management
7. JAN LOGIE (Green)  to the Minister for Social Development : When she said
last month, “for every example that the me mber can give, I can give another 10 of
people who are grateful for the help that th ey are getting” was she saying that it is
acceptable that a large portion of people are not getting the help they are entitled to?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I have seen
absolutely no evidence that there is a larg e portion of people w ho are not getting the
help that they require. In fact, evidence speaks otherwise. For example, access to
hardship assistance has not reduced. Since Sept ember last year, as I have already stated
in the House, benefit numbers have reduced  by 16,500 people, or 5.2 percent. Over that
time grants of hardship assistance have fallen by just 1 percent. The other example is the
triage rates, which are those who go into Work and Income to go on a benefit. For the
last 3 years or 4 years they have averaged around 42 percent; they are currently at about
37 percent. So, actually, more who walk through our door are going on benefit than
were previously 12 months ago. Who we are working more with, though, are people
who have been on longer, putting more support up front around them and doing more
face-to-face interviews, and we are seeing great progress from that.

items.text: What prompted her U-turn on our  request for an evaluation of the

doing pilots. We are testing things. We are pr epared to change. We are always refining.
I think we are having a better look and more tr ansparent look at the welfare system now

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: Well, it is impossible for me to talk about individual
circumstances. If the member really cared, then she would bring them to me and I might

Minister ensure that this evaluation will mean  no more cases such as that of the young
deaf woman who was told she could not ev en apply for the s upport living allowance
because she could speak?

items.speaker: Hon PAULA BENNETT
items.text: I just struggle to believe that that is true. As I say, if the

Immigration, Illegal—Statistics and Costs
8. DENIS O’ROURKE (NZ First)  to the Minister of Immigration : How many
people are currently classified as unlawfully in New Zealand, and what steps, if any, has
he taken to reduce that number?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: The most recent
figure we have is from 2012 and estimates that 14,044—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: How many?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: —14,044—unlawful overstayers were in New
Zealand. This is the lowest number this century  and is more than 20 percent less than in
2007 under the Labour - New Zealand First Government, when—

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. [Interruption]

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: Order! I can anticipate the point of order, but I will hear it from the
member.

items.speaker: Rt Hon Winston Peters
items.text: Great minds think alike. There was no New Zealand First -
Labour coalition Government.

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: It would be helpful to the order of this House if the Minister would
not refer to it as a “Labour - New Zealand First Government”.

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: There were still 3,000 more overstayers in 2007.
To the second part of the question, the Government has incentivised voluntary
departures by banning anyone deported from New Zealand from coming back until they
have repaid the taxpayer for the cost of thei r deportation. Even the n, it is unlikely that
17 Oct 2013 Questions for Oral Answer 14009
they would be let back in. Those and othe r changes have contributed to many more
overstayers choosing to leave voluntarily rather than being forcefully deported.
Denis O’Rourke: If the Government’s policy rega rding people unlawfully in New
Zealand was actually effective, why are the numbers—still at well over 14,000—still so
high?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I would simply dispute the preface to the
question. The numbers are low and dropping.
Denis O’Rourke : Does the Minister accept that the current high level of people
unlawfully in New Zealand and the low proba bility of deportati on constitute a strong
signal to others that they can break immigration law with impunity; if not, why not?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: Well, I simply do not accept that it is high. It is
the lowest figure this century, and continues to drop. It is 23 percent lower than when
that party supported the previous Government.
Denis O’Rourke: What is the estimated cost in term s of health, criminal justice, law
enforcement, education, and other costs associated with people unlawfully in New
Zealand?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I do not have that figure to hand. I would be very
happy to estimate it if the member puts it dow n in a written questi on. But I have every
confidence that it would be at least 23 percent lower than in 2007.
Denis O’Rourke : What steps have been taken to recoup the costs of deporting
people unlawfully in New Zealand, and have those steps been successful?

items.speaker: Hon MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I think it is firstly impor tant to point out that the
removal and deportation costs have halv ed since 2005-06, and the Government has a
very strict policy that nobody may apply for re-entry in to New Zealand until the
taxpayer is refunded the costs of their de portation. That is why, although deportations
have increased slightly, the voluntary departures have more than doubled.
Hawke’s Bay Water Management—Environmental Impact of Plan Change
Proposal
9. Hon RUTH DYSON (Labour—Port Hills)  to the Minister of Conservation :
When was he first informed by the Depart ment of Conservation that they were
considering contributing to any submission on the Tukituki Catchment Proposal that
might include nitrogen and phosphorous management?

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The first full briefing on
Tukituki was on 5 March and it confirmed th e department’s role in the process and
mentioned nitrogen and phosphorous management. The paper was very positive on the
project, saying it offered significant environmental and economic benefits. Let me quote
directly what it said: “An increased and regul ated low-flow level for the Tukituki River
would mitigate the dry condition low-flows which affect native fish and in-stream biota.
Water quality would be improved in the enti re catchment”. If the member read that
report, she would understand w hy I was surprised at the c ontent of the leaked draft
submission, which had a very di fferent view on the effects of  the project. This confirms

submission. The Department of Conservati on has some concerns with the novel

Cabinet made a decision not to proceed w ith a Crown submission. What I would also
draw to the attention of the member is that the former report said that the Department of
Conversation was very positive about the pr oject. The member cannot half quote and
needs to consider all the information.

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Why did he tell the House repeat edly that the first he was aware

items.text: Yes, you do. Let me see what the report on 17 June says. It

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson

items.speaker: Hon Ruth Dyson
items.text: Why did he have Nicky Wagner ask a patsy question on 26
September in order for him to say that se nior management had “not even read the

items.speaker: Hon Dr NICK SMITH
items.text: The reason the member’s question was so useful was that
members opposite selectively ask for just some  of the information. It is important, if
you are going to make a judgment, to have all of the information. For instance, can I

said of me that I did not play any role  in her decision making, that she made the

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speak er. I was actually going to raise

Better Public Services Targets—Rheumatic Fever
10. Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA (National—Maungakiekie) to the Minister of

items.speaker: Health
items.text: What progress is the Government making on its Rheumatic Fever Programme?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: The challenge of reducing rheumatic
fever rates, after years of re lentless increases, is a real challenge. Working with the
Māori Party, an important part of the Government’s campaign to reduce rheumatic fever
rates is easy access local drop-in clinics. Th ese are very important to local families
whose children do not attend schools that ha ve the throat-swabbing services, and for
out-of-time access for all at-risk kids. We can announce today that eight sore throat
drop-in clinics have opened this week, as part of the Government’s $45 million
campaign to reduce rheumatic fever rates, a nd at least 60 more will open in Greater
Auckland and Porirua over the next few months . This is the first time a health system
anywhere in the world has sought to reduce rheumatic fever incidence, and we are
trying numerous innovative ways to achieve this.

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: What particular steps are being taken in Pacific communities
to address unacceptable rheumatic fever rates?

items.speaker: Hon TONY RYALL
items.text: As the member will know, Paci fic children are up to 44 times
more likely to contract rheumatic fever than their non-Pacific classmates. Several
specific strategies are being implemented to  turn this round. Th is afternoon Mrs Turia
will announce that the fight against rheumatic fever is now going door-to-door in the
high-risk areas of Ōtara, Onehunga, Manurewa, Massey, Rānui, and Henderson. Eighty-
two community health workers have alread y been trained, as part of the Pacific
Engagement Strategy, with 23 more due shortly. These health workers will visit around
11,000 at-risk Pacific families in their own hom es and in the community in the Greater
14012 Questions for Oral Answer 17 Oct 2013
Auckland region. Members will be surprised to know that reducing rheumatic fever
rates has been a national prio rity since 2001 and it has only taken this Government to
invest $45 million in this very important programme.

items.speaker: Business

items.text: No specific advice
as yet. However, when reading the membe r’s question this morning, it did give me

Corrections, Department—Staff Safety
12. SCOTT SIMPSON (National—Coromandel)  to the Minister of Corrections :
What recent announcements has she made on improving the safety of Corrections staff?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: Last week I announced plans to
reduce assaults on corrections staff by 50 percent by 2015. This follows the
development of a staff safety plan, review ed by an expert panel chaired by former
Police Commissioner Howard Broad. Change s include increasing training and
mentoring of new custodial staff, piloting a mental health awareness programme for
staff working in high-risk areas, a safety training package for community-based staff,
and improving accessibility of handcuffs for cust odial staff working in high-risk areas.
Offenders can often be dangerous and unpredictable, and this Government is committed
to doing everything we can to ensure the sa fety of staff working in the corrections
environment.

items.speaker: Scott Simpson
items.text: What steps has the Government al ready taken to improve the safety
of staff working with prisoners?

items.speaker: Hon ANNE TOLLEY
items.text: This Government has supporte d a number of new measures
to boost the safety of staff working in pris ons. Last year the Se ntencing (Aggravated
Factors) Amendment Act 2012 was passed, which made offending against a corrections
officer a mandatory aggravating factor at sentencing. We have al so introduced batons,
spit-hoods, and stab-resistant vests for staff working in high-risk situations, and we have
given corrections officers access to pepper spray to use if required. Corrections has also
invested in tactical communications and de-e scalation training for all front-line prison
staff to give them the skills they need to manage a volatile prisoner. Although it is
impossible to eliminate all risks in prison, th is Government is making sure that staff
have the skills to stay safe at work. I seek leave to table two documents that are not
available publicly. These are internal docum ents. The first is a document entitled

items.speaker: Keeping Each Other Safe
items.text: Staff Safety Plan 2013-2014—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER

for Corrections Staff.

objection? There is none. They can be tabled.
Documents, by leave, laid on the Table of the House.

Hon John Banks—Ministerial Resignation

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I have received a letter from Metiria Turei and Grant Robertson
seeking to debate under Standing Order 386 the resignation of the Hon John Banks from
his ministerial portfolios. Th is is a particular case of  recent occurrence involving
ministerial responsibility. Not every ministerial resignation will automatically lead to an
urgent debate being accepted. Having carefu lly considered this application, I have
decided to err on the side of allowing the debate. However, I remind members that the
particular case that has been accepted is the Minister stepping aside from his ministerial
responsibilities. It is not the matters involving the member, which are currently before
the courts. As Mr Robertson acknowledged in his application, the particulars of the case
ought not to be referred to. Although I have discretion under Standing Order 112, I have
not been asked in writing to exercise this di scretion. I therefore inte nd to be vigilant in
ensuring that the House’s rules are followed to the letter.
As Ms Turei’s letter wa s received first, I had earlier accepted her application. I have
therefore allowed her to return to the Chamber at the end of question time, and I call on
Metiria Turei to move that the House ta ke note of an urgent  matter of public
importance.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I move, That the House take note of a
matter of urgent public importance . Disgraced and discredited—this Government is
disgraced and discredited, having  been so reckless as to lose yet another Minister this
term; another Minister. Yes, one is an accident. Two—well, you might be able to justify
two. But now it is three, and possibly another, being return ed to having been disgraced
again. This Government is fragil e, it is in tatters, and we can see that being played out
every day with the desperate measures th at this Government is taking. John Key’s
Government now relies on the votes, on the s upport, of two discredited and disgraced
ex-Ministers, John Banks and Peter Dunne.
The Greens have been very clear from the start: as a result of the reasons behind this
disgrace, and the reasons behind why he ha s resigned as Minister, John Banks must
abstain from voting on National’s sordid Skycity deal—sordid Skycity deal. This
conflict of interest is as bad as it ever gets.

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Sleazy deal.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: I would not be one to comment  on that word. Skycity’s $400
million deal rests on John Banks’ vote. And John Banks’ future as an MP and as a
member of this Parliament rests on Skycity’s  evidence. There is a serious conflict of
interest. John Key has said: “No, nothing to s ee here.” Steven Joyce has confirmed that
yet again today. And yet we know that ther e have been MPs w ho have, rightly and
14016 Urgent Debates 17 Oct 2013
responsibly, declined to vote for legislation concerning casi no deals because they felt
that they had a conflict of interest. This wa s because, in that case, they were receiving
funding from a casino, for various reasons. These MPs did the right thing by saying that
they would not vote for this bill because they  felt that the conflict of interest was too
much. This is a statement of integrity. It is an action of integrity. But what is absolutely
clear from this Government is that it has no integrity, and neither does the disgraced and
discredited John Key.
The Government is now stumbling from cr isis to crisis, it has the thinnest of
majorities, and it is propped up by two lame duck members. New Zealanders are getting
sick and tired of having a failed Government. The good news, of course, is that it is only
a year or so until we get to vote this Government out  and, instead, vote in a Green-
Labour Government with a real plan for New Zealand.
This, of course, is a very long story. We have to remember quite far back to get to the
beginning of this, which is interesting because, of course, it started with John Banks
completely forgetting quite a bit at the time.  He forgot the whole episode. Did he meet
with people and seek donations from them? He could not remember. John Banks forgot.
Did John Banks remember that he got a he licopter ride with Kim Dotcom? No, he
completely forgot about the helicopter ri de. Did he remember the discussion about
getting donations? No, he completely forgot  all about that. Did he remember about
asking for the donations to be anonymous? No, he had no idea. He completely forgot all
about that. But then, of course , he did remember, and was sure  when signing off that he
did not do anything wrong once he had finally remembered. He was sure that he had not
done anything wrong in signing off his electoral  expenses, hence the situation he is
currently in.
How can this Minister have genuinely run successful businesses? And, you know,
John Banks did. He spent two terms as the mayor of New Zealand’s biggest city, he has
been a Minister of the Crown, and he has been an MP in this Parliament for many years,
but how could he have done all of those th ings credibly—and this is the important
issue—knowing that his career and his cred ibility depended on his honesty? He has
signed off on documents that have now led him to be in court on a charge of criminal
fraud. There is an issue here of honesty, an i ssue of credibility, and that has had a very
significant and very negative effect on this Government.
The impact has also been felt by John Ke y. John Key, who refused to read the police
report concerning the case. John Key, who was severe in his criticism of Helen Clark
over the exercise of Taito Phill ip Field’s vote. Some of us in this House may remember
the criticism that John Key made. He dema nded that she abandon the use of Taito
Phillip Field’s vote while he was char ged with and was undergoing the court
proceedings—also criminal court proceedings—that eventually led to his imprisonment.
John Key does not hold himself to the same standard that he requires of other MPs. He
made demands of Helen Clark to force Taito Phillip Field to stand down, to resign, and
to not exercise his vote because he was facing criminal charges. Now he finds himself in
exactly the same position, with a Minister—or  an ex-Minister now, because he has had
to resign—but a member who props up hi s Government and whose proxy vote John
Key and his MPs exercise, and he is quite happy  to continue to exercise that vote while
that member is in court on criminal charges. There is a word for saying one thing and
doing another. [Interruption]

We know that our family members go to the casino and spend money they do not

I think there is great disappointment in J ohn Key and his Government, and there is

New Zealanders deserve a Government that  will legislate for their well-being, for

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: The way the previous member,
Metiria Turei, finished her speech showed  the somewhat unfortunate trend for the
Greens to use more and more extreme language  as they try to co mpete with the Labour
Party for the left-wing vote. It is getting ha rder for the Greens. There is no doubt about

But for a party that came into Parliament to  raise standards, the vicious and vindictive

Mr Banks resigned yesterday, co nsistent with an undertaking he had made that if the

to be commented on have been raised by the previous member and by the Opposition

items.text: Ha! That’s not what you said a few years ago, Bill.

items.text: It is a right of a member of  Parliament to exercise—well,
actually, Phillip Field exercised his vote. He  voted against the Labour Party on some of

As for the Opposition members’ contention that  there is somehow a lack of stability
in the Government, I would invite them, as I did in one of my answers at question time,
to have a look at the confidence and supply agreements that the John Key - led National
Government has in place. In fact, the majo rity of the Governme nt has increased in
recent weeks because Lianne Dalziel has resi gned from Parliament, and we are yet to
see the results of a by-elect ion in Christchurch East. Who knows? The Government’s
majority might increase as a result of that. You just do not know. So the suggestion that

I also want to address one or two other issues that the member for the Greens
actually raised. One of them, which I thought was quite out of  order, was the assertion
that the Government is somehow failing da y by day. When the economy is growing;
when employment in the region s is picking up; when it is pretty clear that in every
region, despite the reces sion, the economy grew; when the numbers grew in all except
one region—that is Gisborne—when we see re ports today that in the South Island job
vacancies are booming; they are not signs of a failing economy or of a failing
Government.
I would also invite the member from the Greens, who decided to focus not so much
on the capacities of Mr Banks but on the capa cities of other Minist ers, to look a bit
more closely at policy. In fact, I would invite  the Greens to think pretty hard about their
own consciences. In respect of  education, both the previous Minister and the current
Minister have done more than any Green-Labour Government did to focus on those who
most need the benefits of public educati on—who most need the benefits of public
education. The Greens have opposed every single policy that is going about the difficult
task of providing for thos e who most need the opportuni ty of a good education and a
better opportunity. We will stand by that, whatever ministerial resignations there are.
To come back to Mr Banks, he has perf ormed his duties as a Minister with
consistency. He has stuck to the confiden ce and supply agreement. I have dealt with
him over regulatory issues. They are comple x. The Labour Party just agrees on more
and more regulation; Mr Banks does not. He agrees with sensible regulation, and we
have worked quite hard, actually, to create a regulatory system that deals with the issues

would have, among Governments across the world, one of the more progressive
approaches to regulation. That is evident.  As for small business, John Banks was a
strong advocate for things like a 90-day trial period, which encourages employment in

able to negotiate to set their own wages. It wants the living wage for all small
businesses, particularly retail and those that service the Government. John Banks stood
by those businesses.
So it is of some regret to the Government that John Banks has resigned as a Minister,
because he carried out his duties faithfull y. Sometimes he had differences of opinion
with the Government, but, nevertheless, he stuck to advocating for those groups that
would expect a Minister in that portfolio to advocate. Now, as with any New Zealand
citizen who faces an allegation of unlawful  behaviour, he will have to go through the
legal process. He has outlined his own position about that, but it is appropriate that he
ceases to function as a Minister while that is under way.
